title: Fainting on the toilet three days after a visit for constipation

source.citation: Jones DD, Kummer T, Schoen JC. Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy with an Intrauterine Device: Case Report and Sonographic Considerations. Clin Pract Cases Emerg Med. 2020;4(4):559-563.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Fainted on the toilet; abdominal pain
presentation.hpi: Three days ago she was seen at an urgent care clinic for constipation and sent home with lactulose. The next day she developed abdominal cramps and several near-fainting spells. Today, after a dose of lactulose, she had sudden diarrhea with worsening abdominal pain and briefly lost consciousness while seated on the toilet, without injury. Her last menstrual period was about a month ago, and she has a levonorgestrel intrauterine device for contraception. No fever, vomiting or vaginal bleeding.
meds: Lactulose (prescribed 3 days ago at urgent care)

exam: Awake, alert and in no distress
Abdomen soft and mildly distended with diffuse tenderness; no guarding
After a 1 L normal saline bolus: blood pressure 101/55 mm Hg

imaging.finding: Free fluid in the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch)
IUD within the uterus; no intrauterine pregnancy; free fluid behind the uterus
10-cm heterogeneous mass posterior to the uterus, moderate free pelvic fluid, no intrauterine pregnancy and no adnexal abnormality; IUD well positioned in the endometrial canal

ecg: Sinus rhythm 84/min, normal intervals, no pre-excitation or ischemic changes

diagnosis.primary: Ruptured abdominal ectopic pregnancy (posterior cul-de-sac) with hemoperitoneum, despite a well-positioned levonorgestrel IUD
differentials: Splenic rupture or other intra-abdominal bleeding

management: Cardiac monitoring, peripheral IV access and a 1 L normal saline bolus (BP 78/64 to 101/55 mm Hg)
Bedside ultrasound (right upper quadrant and transabdominal pelvic) while the urine pregnancy test was pending
On-call obstetrician consulted in the ED; formal transvaginal ultrasound

Because the retro-uterine mass raised concern for other pathology such as malignancy, transfer to a tertiary center by air ambulance; repeat hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, transfusion of 1 unit of packed red cells started

Referral ED: BP 119/54 mm Hg, HR 82/min; emergency operation found extensive hemoperitoneum and organized clot behind the uterus, and an abdominal implantation site in the posterior cul-de-sac (medial to the left uterosacral ligament) that was excised and confirmed by pathology
Intramuscular methotrexate because of the abdominal implantation site, with hCG followed to negative
outcome: Uncomplicated recovery: discharged the same day as surgery; after methotrexate, hCG was negative about 4 weeks later.
teachingPoints: Test for pregnancy in every woman of reproductive age with syncope or abdominal pain, even with highly effective contraception: when an IUD fails, the pregnancy is disproportionately likely to be extrauterine.
Tachycardia is often absent in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; hemoperitoneum can cause a relative bradycardia, so a normal heart rate does not exclude major bleeding.
In suspected ectopic pregnancy, an empty uterus plus free fluid in Morison's pouch on bedside ultrasound is highly specific for rupture and predicts the need for surgery.
IUD-associated ectopic pregnancies implant more often at distal sites (ovary, abdomen); normal adnexa on transvaginal ultrasound do not exclude an extrauterine pregnancy.
Hemodynamic instability or hemoperitoneum means surgery, not methotrexate, and confirmatory imaging or transfer should not delay it.

questions.q: While the urine pregnancy test is pending, what is the most useful immediate bedside investigation?
options: Point-of-care ultrasound for free intraperitoneal fluid
CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
Plain abdominal radiograph for stool burden or obstruction
Serum quantitative β-hCG before deciding on ultrasound
questions.explanation: Syncope, abdominal pain and hypotension in a woman of reproductive age suggest hemoperitoneum, and bedside ultrasound can show free fluid within minutes during resuscitation. The β-hCG level should not decide whether a symptomatic patient is scanned (ACEP 2017 clinical policy on early pregnancy), and CT takes an unstable patient out of the resuscitation bay.

questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.extra: Urine pregnancy test positive. Hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL. Bedside ultrasound: free fluid in Morison's pouch; IUD in the uterus; no intrauterine pregnancy.
options: Uterine perforation by the IUD with bleeding
questions.explanation: A positive pregnancy test, an empty uterus and free fluid in Morison's pouch is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise, and the combination predicts the need for surgery. A pregnancy that occurs with an IUD in place is much more likely than usual to be extrauterine, even when the IUD is correctly positioned.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.extra: Transvaginal ultrasound: 10-cm heterogeneous mass behind the uterus, moderate free pelvic fluid, normal adnexa, no intrauterine pregnancy. Repeat hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL; BP 101/55 mm Hg after 1 L of saline.
options: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate with hCG on days 4 and 7
Expectant management with serial hemoglobin and hCG levels
MRI of the pelvis to characterize the mass before intervening
Blood transfusion and emergency laparoscopy or laparotomy
questions.explanation: Hemoperitoneum with a falling hemoglobin needs blood and an operation; ruptured ectopic pregnancy and hemodynamic instability are contraindications to methotrexate (ACOG Practice Bulletin 193). Normal adnexa do not exclude an abdominal implantation, which IUD-associated pregnancies favor, and more imaging only delays surgery.

questions.q: How should her heart rate of 84/min be interpreted alongside a blood pressure of 78/64 mm Hg?
options: It argues against bleeding and favors a cardiac cause of syncope
A normal heart rate does not exclude major intraperitoneal bleeding
It means the hypotension is probably a cuff artifact to recheck later
It suggests hormonal blunting of the stress response by the IUD
questions.explanation: Many patients with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy are not tachycardic; blood in the peritoneum can cause a vagally mediated relative bradycardia, and in one cited study only 12% presented with both tachycardia and hypotension. Hypotension with syncope in early pregnancy should be treated as hemorrhage.

evidence.quote: A healthy 21-year-old female presented to the local community ED for evaluation of syncope and abdominal pain.
She had been evaluated at the local urgent care three days prior, complaining of constipation and was discharged with a prescription for lactulose.
The following day she developed abdominal cramping and several near-syncopal spells.
developed sudden onset diarrhea and worsening abdominal pain. While seated on the toilet, she suffered a brief syncopal episode without associated trauma.
her last menstrual period was one month prior and that she had a levonorgestrel IUD in place for contraception
She reported no fever, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding.
On arrival in the ED, the patient was awake, alert, and in no distress.
temperature of 36.5º Celsius, heart rate of 84 beats per minute, blood pressure of 78/64 millimeters of mercury
respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 100% on room air
her abdomen was soft and mildly distended with diffuse tenderness to palpation; she had no guarding
The patient was maintained on a cardiac monitor, and a peripheral intravenous line was established.
She was resuscitated with one liter normal saline bolus and her blood pressure improved to 101/55 mm Hg.
hemoglobin 7.9 grams (g) per deciliter (dL) (reference [ref] range: 12.0–15.5 g/dL) and hematocrit 23.4%
Her electrolytes, blood glucose, and lactate were unremarkable.
POCUS was notable for free fluid in the hepatorenal recess (Morison’s pouch) in the right upper quadrant
Transabdominal point-of-care pelvic ultrasound demonstrated an IUD, but no visible intrauterine pregnancy (IUP)
an intrauterine device within the uterus (arrow), no evidence of intrauterine pregnancy, and free fluid posterior to the uterus
Subsequently, the urine pregnancy test result returned and was positive.
The obstetric physician on-call was consulted, evaluated the patient in the ED, reviewed the POCUS images, and requested comprehensive transvaginal (TV) ultrasound
This demonstrated a 10-centimeter heterogeneous mass posterior to the uterus, moderate free fluid in the pelvis, and no evidence of intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) or adnexal abnormality.
The IUD was noted to be in good position in the endometrial canal.
raised concern for alternate pathology (such as malignancy) … the decision was made to transfer the patient to the regional tertiary care center
Repeat hemoglobin was 6.2 g/dL (ref range: 12.0–15.5 g/dL). Transfusion with one unit of packed red blood cells was initiated, and she was transferred via air ambulance.
On arrival to the referral ED, she was hemodynamically stable with a blood pressure of 119/54 mm Hg and a heart rate of 82 beats per minute.
She was noted to have extensive hemoperitoneum and organized clot posterior to the uterus.
the site of the ectopic pregnancy appeared to be abdominal in the posterior cul de sac medial to the left uterosacral ligament and lateral to the rectum
This was excised and later confirmed by pathology.
We present a rare case of ruptured abdominal ectopic pregnancy in a patient with a well-positioned IUD.
The patient tolerated the procedure well and was discharged later that day.
she was treated with intramuscular methotrexate and followed until beta human gonadotropin (hCG) levels were negative approximately four weeks later
